topic: Tulip Mania and the World's First Economic Crash

text.content: During the 1630s, the Netherlands was one of the richest trading nations in the world. Its wealthy citizens were always looking for beautiful new items to display in their homes and gardens to show off their money. During this time, trading ships brought a completely new, brightly colored flower from Turkey. This beautiful, exotic flower quickly became a symbol of extreme wealth. It was known as the tulip.

While normal tulips were expensive, a very rare type of the flower became incredibly valuable. A strange biological virus caused the petals of some flowers to grow beautiful, flame-like stripes of red and white. Because no one knew how to grow these striped flowers on purpose, they were incredibly rare. Rich merchants were willing to pay huge amounts of money just to own a single striped bulb.

Soon, regular people realized they could make a lot of money by trading these flowers. Shoemakers, farmers, and bakers began selling their tools and houses just to buy a few flower bulbs. They planned to hold onto the bulbs for a few weeks and sell them to someone else for a much higher price. At the peak of this madness, a single rare flower bulb cost as much as a large luxury house in the center of the city.

However, this insane financial system could not last forever. In February 1637, a group of buyers suddenly refused to pay the high prices. Panic quickly spread across the country, and everyone tried to sell their flowers at the exact same time. Within a few days, the price of the flowers dropped to almost zero, completely ruining the families who had sold their homes. This sudden and disastrous financial crash is known today by a specific term. It is called an economic bubble.

The disaster of the flowers taught the world a very painful lesson about human greed. It proved that when people buy things only because they think the price will go up, the market will eventually crash. Today, modern economists still study the events of 1637 to understand how public panic can destroy financial markets. It is remembered as the first major financial crash in recorded history.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B states the exact opposite: 'Because no one knew how to grow these striped flowers on purpose, they were incredibly rare.'
